## Dismissal as defense minister (October 2023)

On Tuesday, October 24, 2023, China announced that Li had been dismissed as defense minister after nearly two months out of public view.[{n}] Just four months earlier he had appeared at a regional security forum in Singapore as the face of Beijing's bold vision for reshaping Asia's balance of power, casting China as a force for stability and accusing the United States of stirring trouble in the region, with the suggestion that Washington should "mind your own business."[{n}]

Li, appointed in March 2023, was the second senior Chinese official purged that year without explanation and under a cloud of suspicion, following the July dismissal of foreign minister [[qin-gang|Qin Gang]].[{n}] His removal also came after an abrupt August 2023 shake-up in the leadership of China's nuclear force, described as the highest-level upheaval in the Chinese military in recent years.[{n}] American officials had said the previous month that Chinese authorities placed Li under investigation over corruption, and the announcement left open whether he was being probed for any offenses.[{n}]

[[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] argued that Western coverage of the firing — including [[new-york-times|New York Times]] framing about the "capriciousness of high-level politics in China under Xi Jinping" — reflected the assumptions of legacy media rather than the facts, and that the purges underway in China, Russia and Ukraine were not going the way those outlets would prefer.[{n}]

## The 2023 purges of senior officials

In 2023 Xi presided over the unexplained removal of two senior officials: foreign minister [[qin-gang|Qin Gang]] in July, amid speculation about a compromising affair during his ambassadorship in Washington, and defense minister [[li-shangfu|Gen. Li Shangfu]] in October, after nearly two months of public absence and reported corruption investigation.[{n}] The removals followed an abrupt August 2023 shake-up in the leadership of China's nuclear force, the highest-level upheaval in the Chinese military in recent years.[{n}]

Western outlets presented the sequence as evidence of the opacity of high-level politics under Xi and framed his long-running anti-corruption campaign as cover for removing officials disloyal to his vision for China.[{n}] Badlands contributor [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] rejected that framing as "Hegelian illusionists allowing audience assumptions to color their version of the truth," comparing it to the treatment of [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] as a threat to "their Democracy."[{n}]

## October 2023 drone attacks on Iraq and Syria bases

CENTCOM told NBC News on Tuesday, October 24, 2023, that two dozen American military personnel had been wounded the previous week in a series of drone attacks on American bases in Iraq and Syria.[{n}] [[pentagon|The Pentagon]] had confirmed the attacks the week before, but the casualty count had not previously been disclosed.[{n}]

According to CENTCOM, twenty American personnel sustained minor injuries on October 18 when at least two one-way attack drones targeted the [[al-tanf-garrison|al-Tanf military base]] in southern Syria; one drone was shot down, all wounded personnel returned to duty, and no military installations were damaged.[{n}] That same day, four American personnel suffered minor injuries in two separate drone attacks on U.S. and coalition forces at [[ain-al-asad-airbase|al-Asad base]] in western Iraq.[{n}]

## Warning on Iranian proxies (October 2023)

In late October 2023 Blinken warned of "decisive action" should U.S. troops be threatened any further by Iranian proxies operating in the Middle East.[{n}] Within hours, [[pentagon|the Pentagon]] and [[us-central-command|CENTCOM]] disclosed that two dozen American personnel had already been wounded in drone attacks on bases in Iraq and Syria, apparently emanating from those same sources.[{n}]

Badlands contributor [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]], referring to him as "Secretary of (Deep) State," argued that the [[joe-biden|Biden]] administration and the [[state-department|State Department]] had refused to entertain ceasefire proposals, warned of decisive action in the event of escalation, and were then promptly greeted with that escalation — a pattern he read as either the [[hegelian-dialectic|Hegelian dialectic]] playing out in full view of the American public or an administration with no idea how to manage a chaos it found unwieldy, producing contradictory statements on a near-hourly basis.[{n}]

## Middle East escalation messaging (October 2023)

In October 2023 the State Department under Secretary [[antony-blinken|Antony Blinken]] warned of "decisive action" if U.S. troops faced further threats from Iranian proxies, only for [[pentagon|the Pentagon]] to report shortly afterward that two dozen American personnel had already been wounded in drone attacks on bases in Iraq and Syria.[{n}] Badlands commentary held that the department and the wider [[joe-biden|Biden]] administration refused to dwell on "such trivial, naive concerns as ceasefires," warned of escalation, and were then met with it — behaviour read as either deliberate [[hegelian-dialectic|Hegelian]] narrative management or simple incoherence.[{n}]

## October 2023 drone attack casualties and the Israel stockpile

The Pentagon confirmed in mid-October 2023 a series of drone attacks on American bases in Iraq and Syria but did not initially disclose casualties; [[us-central-command|CENTCOM]] later told NBC News that two dozen U.S. military personnel had been wounded, twenty at [[al-tanf-garrison|al-Tanf]] in Syria and four at [[ain-al-asad-airbase|al-Asad]] in Iraq.[{n}]

Separately, at a Pentagon press conference on Monday, October 23, 2023, a senior defense official acknowledged that the [[department-of-defense|Department of Defense]] was returning to Israel 155 mm artillery shells it had earlier withdrawn from its stockpile in Israel for U.S. forces in European Command: "We withdrew 155 [shells] from the stockpile in Israel for our forces in [European Command] and now we are sending that back to Israel for their use."[{n}] The Pentagon had first acknowledged in January that it dipped into the Israel stockpile to supply Ukraine, and the [[new-york-times|New York Times]] reported that "half" of the shells there were shipped to Europe the previous winter.[{n}]

## Return of Ukraine-diverted munitions to Israel (October 2023)

On Monday, October 23, 2023, the Department of Defense admitted it was sending back to Israel some of the weapons it had drawn from its stockpiles there and shipped to Europe for Ukraine, while insisting it could supply both conflicts.[{n}] A senior defense official told reporters at a [[pentagon|Pentagon]] press briefing: "We withdrew 155 [shells] from the stockpile in Israel for our forces in [European Command] and now we are sending that back to Israel for their use."[{n}]

The department had first acknowledged in January 2023 that, to supply Ukraine with 155 mm artillery shells for its ground war with Russia, it dipped into the U.S. stockpile maintained in Israel.[{n}] That stockpile exists for American forces in the region but also for Israeli forces in emergencies such as the October 7, 2023 [[hamas|Hamas]] attacks, after which the United States flew additional weapons to Israel.[{n}] The [[new-york-times|New York Times]] reported that "half" of the shells in the Israel stockpile had been shipped to Europe the previous winter.[{n}]

Badlands contributor [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] wrote that the United States relocated much of that stockpile to [[volodymyr-zelensky|Zelenskyy]] during the "Slava Ukraine! psyop" and was now sending it back, remarking that "it's almost as if the US has no standards in who they support," and noting that Republicans in [[us-congress|Congress]] were pushing to separate additional Ukraine funding from Israel aid — a move Senator [[john-fetterman|John Fetterman]] answered on X with "F*ck that."[{n}] She added that everything the Biden administration and the 118th Congress did appeared to be an escalation, and asked, "What's the carbon footprint of World War III?"[{n}]

## US munitions transfers and the Israel stockpile (October 2023)

Badlands commentary in October 2023 tied Zelenskyy directly to the [[department-of-defense|Department of Defense]]'s admission that it was returning to Israel 155 mm artillery shells previously drawn from the American stockpile in Israel and shipped to Europe for Ukraine.[{n}] Contributor [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] characterized the transfer as part of a "Slava Ukraine! psyop" that had relocated much of that stockpile to "Zelenskyy and his Azov bros," and argued the reversal showed the United States had no consistent standard governing whom it arms.[{n}]

## Speaker vacancy and aid standoff (October 2023)

By late October 2023 the House had gone three weeks without a Speaker following the removal of [[kevin-mccarthy|Kevin McCarthy]], with House Republicans on Tuesday, October 24 selecting [[mike-johnson|Mike Johnson]] as their fourth nominee after Majority Whip [[tom-emmer|Tom Emmer]]'s bid collapsed the same day.[{n}] Badlands contributor [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] argued that "the longer the House goes without a Speaker, the better off Americans will be" because "the gridlock favors the people," promoting the hashtag #vacatecongress.[{n}]

During the same period Republicans in Congress pressed to separate additional Ukraine funding from Israel aid, a demand Senator [[john-fetterman|John Fetterman]] answered publicly with "F*ck that."[{n}] Badlands commentary held that everything the [[joe-biden|Biden]] administration and the 118th Congress did at that point amounted to escalation on at least two fronts.[{n}]

## Fourth nominee: Mike Johnson (October 24, 2023)

On Tuesday evening, October 24, 2023, House Republicans picked Rep. [[mike-johnson|Mike Johnson]] (R-La.) as their fourth nominee for Speaker, just hours after House Majority Whip [[tom-emmer|Tom Emmer]] (R-Minn.) ended his bid.[{n}] Emmer had won the conference nomination after five rounds of voting but withdrew once it became clear he would face too many opponents to reach 217 votes on the House floor.[{n}] Johnson won 128 votes in conference that night, well short of the 217 required on the floor, and the House had by then been without a Speaker for three weeks.[{n}]

No floor vote was held that Tuesday.[{n}] Badlands contributor [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] described the day as "a rollercoaster" and reported a rumor on the Hill that [[kevin-mccarthy|Kevin McCarthy]] would come back up for a vote — a prediction she credited to Badlands' own [[canncon|CannCon]] on the day McCarthy was ousted.[{n}] With the House due to reassemble Wednesday at noon, she wrote that those paying attention were not holding their breath, and argued that "the longer the House goes without a Speaker, the better off Americans will be. The gridlock favors the people."[{n}]

## Selection as fourth speaker nominee (October 24, 2023)

On the evening of Tuesday, October 24, 2023, House Republicans picked Johnson as their fourth nominee for Speaker, hours after Majority Whip [[tom-emmer|Tom Emmer]] withdrew following his own nomination win.[{n}] Johnson took 128 votes in the conference ballot, far short of the 217 needed on the House floor, and it remained unclear at that point whether he could reach the threshold.[{n}] The House had been without a Speaker for three weeks since the removal of [[kevin-mccarthy|Kevin McCarthy]], and was set to reassemble Wednesday at noon.[{n}] See [[2023-speaker-of-the-house-election]].[{n}]

## Collapse of the October 24, 2023 nomination

Emmer won the House Republican conference's speaker nomination after five rounds of voting on Tuesday, October 24, 2023, but withdrew hours later once it became clear the Minnesota lawmaker would face too many opponents to reach 217 votes on the House floor.[{n}] Republicans that evening turned to [[mike-johnson|Mike Johnson]] as their fourth nominee, who won 128 conference votes.[{n}] Badlands contributor [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] called the day "a rollercoaster," noting that no floor vote was held and that rumors on the Hill had [[kevin-mccarthy|Kevin McCarthy]] returning for another vote.[{n}]

## Speculation about a return (October 2023)

During the fourth round of the speakership contest on October 24, 2023, Badlands contributor [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] reported a rumor circulating on Capitol Hill that McCarthy would come back up for a vote — a scenario she noted had been predicted by Badlands' [[canncon|CannCon]] on the very day McCarthy was ousted.[{n}] The House had at that point gone three weeks without a Speaker following his removal, with [[tom-emmer|Tom Emmer]]'s bid collapsing and [[mike-johnson|Mike Johnson]] emerging as the conference's fourth nominee.[{n}]

## Response to splitting Ukraine and Israel aid (October 2023)

When Republicans in [[us-congress|Congress]] pushed in October 2023 to separate additional Ukraine funding from Israel aid, Fetterman posted a two-word reply on X: "F*ck that."[{n}] He did not elaborate.[{n}] Badlands contributor [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] cited the post — describing him as "the ever-eloquent Senator John Fetterman (D-PA)" — as an illustration of a Congress she argued was uniformly committed to escalation on at least two fronts.[{n}]

## State objections to the Epstein settlement (October 2023)

JPMorgan Chase's $290 million class-action settlement with accusers of [[jeffrey-epstein|Jeffrey Epstein]] drew an objection from many U.S. states in October 2023, on the grounds that the accord could limit their ability to seek compensation for sexual abuse victims.[{n}] In a letter made public on Monday, October 23 in Manhattan federal court, the attorneys general of 16 states and Washington, D.C. complained about settlement language preventing "any sovereign or government" from seeking damages arising from sex trafficking by Epstein and his associates.[{n}]

The attorneys general said that including such language without their consent would deter them from seeking damages for sex trafficking victims — not only Epstein's — under the federal [[trafficking-victims-protection-act|Trafficking Victims Protection Act]].[{n}] They also observed that [[deutsche-bank|Deutsche Bank]]'s similar $75 million agreement with Epstein's accusers contained no such language.[{n}] New Mexico Attorney General [[raul-torrez|Raul Torrez]] wrote that Epstein's surviving victims "should be fully compensated for the profound harm they have suffered," but that the agreement "improperly seeks to release (the states') claims for victim-specific relief."[{n}] Signatories included Arizona, California, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Minnesota, Mississippi, New York, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Utah and Vermont.[{n}]

## State objections to bank settlements (October 2023)

In October 2023 the attorneys general of 16 states and Washington, D.C. objected to [[jpmorgan-chase|JPMorgan Chase]]'s $290 million class-action settlement with Epstein's accusers, arguing that language barring "any sovereign or government" from seeking damages arising from sex trafficking by Epstein and his associates could bar states from pursuing victim-specific relief under the federal [[trafficking-victims-protection-act|Trafficking Victims Protection Act]].[{n}] The letter, made public in Manhattan federal court, noted that [[deutsche-bank|Deutsche Bank]]'s $75 million settlement with Epstein accusers — approved days earlier — contained no comparable release.[{n}] New Mexico Attorney General [[raul-torrez|Raul Torrez]] argued the accord "improperly seeks to release (the states') claims for victim-specific relief."[{n}]

## Epstein settlement comparison (October 2023)

A federal judge approved Deutsche Bank's $75 million settlement with accusers of [[jeffrey-epstein|Jeffrey Epstein]] on October 20, 2023.[{n}] Days later, state attorneys general objecting to [[jpmorgan-chase|JPMorgan Chase]]'s larger $290 million settlement cited the Deutsche Bank agreement favourably, noting that it did not contain the language barring "any sovereign or government" from seeking damages arising from Epstein-related sex trafficking that they found objectionable in the JPMorgan accord.[{n}]

## Arlington Assembly walkout (October 24, 2023)

On Tuesday, October 24, 2023, [[united-auto-workers|UAW]] president [[shawn-fain|Shawn Fain]] hit [[general-motors|General Motors]]' largest and most profitable SUV plant with a surprise 5,000-member strike, escalating the union's stand-up strike strategy against Detroit's Big Three.[{n}] The walkout followed news the previous day that the union had struck [[stellantis|Stellantis]]' RAM 1500 truck plant in Michigan.[{n}]

The GM Arlington Assembly plant manufactures the Chevy Tahoe, Chevy Suburban, GMC Yukon and Cadillac Escalade.[{n}] The strike announcement came hours after GM reported quarterly profits exceeding expectations while retracting its full-year forecast, citing anticipated fourth-quarter financial challenges as the strike approached its sixth week.[{n}] "Another record quarter, another record year. As we've said for months: record profits equal record contracts," Fain said, adding, "It's time GM workers, and the whole working class, get their fair share."[{n}]

## Surprise strike at GM Arlington (October 2023)

On Tuesday, October 24, 2023, Fain called a surprise 5,000-member strike at [[general-motors|General Motors]]' largest and most profitable SUV plant, one day after the [[united-auto-workers|UAW]] struck [[stellantis|Stellantis]]' RAM 1500 truck plant in Michigan.[{n}] The action came hours after GM reported quarterly profits that topped estimates while withdrawing its full-year forecast.[{n}] "Another record quarter, another record year. As we've said for months: record profits equal record contracts," Fain said, adding that "it's time GM workers, and the whole working class, get their fair share."[{n}] See [[2023-united-auto-workers-strike]].[{n}]

## Escalation against GM and Stellantis (October 2023)

In the sixth week of its 2023 stand-up strike campaign, the UAW under president [[shawn-fain|Shawn Fain]] struck [[stellantis|Stellantis]]' RAM 1500 truck plant in Michigan on Monday, October 23, 2023, and followed on Tuesday with a surprise 5,000-worker walkout at [[general-motors|General Motors]]' Arlington Assembly plant, the automaker's largest and most profitable SUV facility.[{n}] The union framed the escalation around GM's better-than-expected quarterly profits, with Fain arguing that "record profits equal record contracts."[{n}] See [[2023-united-auto-workers-strike]].[{n}]

## Arlington Assembly strike (October 2023)

On October 24, 2023, the [[united-auto-workers|UAW]] struck GM's Arlington Assembly plant — the company's largest and most profitable SUV facility, producing the Chevy Tahoe, Chevy Suburban, GMC Yukon and Cadillac Escalade — with a surprise 5,000-member walkout.[{n}] The strike was announced hours after GM reported quarterly profits exceeding expectations while withdrawing its full-year forecast, citing anticipated financial challenges in the fourth quarter as the labor action approached its sixth week.[{n}] Union president [[shawn-fain|Shawn Fain]] said "record profits equal record contracts."[{n}] See [[2023-united-auto-workers-strike]].[{n}]

## RAM 1500 plant strike (October 2023)

On Monday, October 23, 2023, the [[united-auto-workers|UAW]] struck Stellantis' RAM 1500 truck plant in Michigan, one day before president [[shawn-fain|Shawn Fain]] escalated further with a surprise 5,000-worker walkout at [[general-motors|General Motors]]' Arlington Assembly plant.[{n}] The back-to-back actions marked an acceleration of the union's rolling strike strategy against Detroit's Big Three in the sixth week of the dispute.[{n}] See [[2023-united-auto-workers-strike]].[{n}]

## COVID-19 vaccine injury payments (October 2023)

HRSA, which runs the [[countermeasures-injury-compensation-program|Countermeasures Injury Compensation Program]] (CICP), disclosed in an update reflecting data current as of October 1, 2023 that it had paid two more people injured by COVID-19 vaccines.[{n}] Both had experienced myocarditis, or heart inflammation, after vaccination; one received $4,183 and the other $4,934.[{n}] The agency declined to disclose which shots the recipients had received and did not respond to requests for more information.[{n}] The payments came as HRSA faced the prospect of being forced by a court to improve the program for victims, and critics said the sums fell far short of satisfying calls to reform the government's handling of vaccine injuries.[{n}]

## 2023 media confidence survey

Gallup's annual survey of trust in U.S. institutions, conducted September 1–23, 2023, found Americans' confidence that mass media — newspapers, television and radio — would report the news fully, accurately and fairly had plummeted to lows matching the previous record set in 2016.[{n}] Twenty-nine percent of U.S. adults reported "not very much" trust in the media, while a record-high 39 percent reported "none at all" — one percentage point above the previous record and 12 points higher than the 2016 reading, when the most common sentiment was "not very much" trust at 41 percent.[{n}] Gallup characterized the result as the grimmest view of the media in its polling history, part of a half-century of steadily declining trust.[{n}] The 2016 low had coincided with sharp criticism of the press from then-candidate [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]].[{n}]

Badlands contributor [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] read the collapse as a precondition for narrative change, writing that before the American public can be told a new story "buoyed by the truth," they must first disengage from the current story and its storytellers — and that the data showed they were doing so.[{n}] He closed by asking readers to recall what happened in 2016, the last time public trust in the Central Narrative was this low.[{n}]
